description: Somos un equipo de niños y jóvenes de ROBOKIDS unidos por un mismo sueño, demostrar nuestro talento y descubrir hasta dónde podemos llegar. Creemos que la edad no define nuestras capacidades y que las grandes ideas pueden nacer en cualquier lugar. Hoy, en el NASA Space Apps Challenge, queremos aprender, crear y demostrar que con pasión, esfuerzo y trabajo en equipo, los sueños que parecen lejanos pueden convertirse en el comienzo de algo extraordinario.
summary:
AstroHealth Guardian is a visual self-check tool that helps astronauts look after their own health on long missions, when a doctor on Earth may be minutes away. We focus on breathing and mental health, linked to NASA Human Research Program risks: hypoxia, behavioral changes and inadequate sleep.

Each day a crew member records indicators such as breathing rate, oxygen saturation, heart rate, sleep, mood and stress, by hand, with a built-in breathing counter, or from a USB or Bluetooth sensor. The app compares them with that person's own baseline from their pre-flight medical record, colors a clickable body map green, yellow or red, explains why, and says what to do next with short guide videos and exercises.

Red results create an alert for a Ground Control view. If the link with Earth is lost, data is stored on board and sent when the link returns. The tool also includes on-board emergency protocols, a medical inventory, and letters from home to support the crew's mood. It works offline in English and Spanish.

Crews going to the Moon and Mars must notice changes in themselves early. All data in this prototype is simulated, including sensor values, and the tool guides but does not diagnose.
details:
WHAT IT DOES AND HOW IT WORKS

AstroHealth Guardian is a self-check tool that lets an astronaut review their own health in a few minutes and know what to do next. The crew member completes a daily check-in with breathing rate, oxygen saturation, heart rate, blood pressure, temperature, blood sugar, sleep, mood, stress and exercise. Values can be typed, counted with a built-in breathing counter, or received from a sensor by USB or Bluetooth.

The app compares each value with that person's own baseline: first the pre-flight values in their medical record, and after three check-ins, their in-flight average. An interactive body map of the head and torso turns green, yellow or red for five systems (lungs, mind, heart, bones, immune system and nutrition). For each one the app explains why it has that color and what to do, with step-by-step guides, short animated videos and exercises.

When a system turns red, an alert is created for a Ground Control view. The signal delay is calculated from the distance of the selected environment (space station, Moon, Mars transit or Mars). If the link with Earth is lost, check-ins and alerts stay on board and are sent when the link returns.

The tool also includes medical records that are updated before each mission and saved as versions, on-board emergency protocols, a ship medical inventory, messages from Earth, and letters from home that the crew can save and read to support their mood.

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT

On long missions the crew carries much of the responsibility for spotting changes in themselves. Our tool turns numbers into a clear color, a reason and an action, without assuming medical training. Comparing each person with their own baseline avoids one limit for everyone. Because it works offline, it keeps helping when communication is delayed or lost. The same idea could help people on Earth who live far from medical care.

TOOLS, LANGUAGES AND HARDWARE

- Front end: one HTML file with CSS and JavaScript, no external libraries, body map drawn in SVG.

- Back end: Python with Flask and an SQLite database that stores check-ins, alerts and medical records.

- Sensors: Web Bluetooth and Web Serial. An ESP32 board programmed with Arduino sends readings by USB; a button on the board triggers a breathing problem to demonstrate an alert. The circuit was also simulated in Wokwi.

- Guide videos generated by code with Python, with no people or photos.

- Languages in the interface: English and Spanish.

HOW IT IS CREATIVE

We focused on breathing and mental health instead of a general dashboard, and connected them: sleep, stress and breathing are shown together, and the response to a yellow or red result can be a guided breathing exercise. We designed for the moment when Earth cannot answer, and we added human support such as letters from home, because mental health is not only numbers.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

- Communication delay and loss of signal.

- Astronauts are not doctors, so every result has a plain explanation.

- Individual differences: research shows some differences between women and men in spaceflight but limited data, so we use personal baselines.

- Privacy: a call-sign mode hides real names.

- International crews: two languages.

- Honesty: all crew data and sensor values in this prototype are simulated, the color limits are demonstration values and not medical limits, and the tool guides but does not diagnose or prescribe.

USE OF AI TOOLS

This project was built with AI assistance. Gemini was used for the first visual prototype, and Claude (Anthropic) for software development, code review, the script that generates the guide videos, and editing of texts and translations. The team defined the idea, the focus on breathing and mental health, the features, and tested the prototype. No AI-generated images, audio or video models were used, and no NASA logos or branding appear in the project.
